paragraphs.heading: Red corundum
paragraphs.text: Ruby is a gemstone colored pinkish-red to blood-red. It is a variety of the mineral corundum, which consists of aluminium oxide. Other gem-quality varieties of corundum are called sapphires. Ruby is very durable and is among the most popular traditional jewelry gems. Its name comes from ruber, the Latin word for red.

paragraphs.heading: Only two natural gems are harder
paragraphs.text: On the Mohs scale of mineral hardness, rubies score 9.0. Only two natural gems are harder: moissanite and diamond. Diamond has a Mohs hardness of 10.0, and moissanite falls somewhere between corundum and diamond.

paragraphs.heading: Why chromium makes it red
paragraphs.text: Pure corundum is perfectly colorless. Ruby's color is due to chromium. Now and then a chromium atom takes the place of an aluminium atom, and it loses 3 electrons to become a Cr³⁺ ion. The Cr³⁺ ions are larger than aluminium, the O²⁻ ions' octahedral arrangement gets distorted, and the energy levels of the Cr³⁺ ions' orbitals are slightly altered. Those energy differences match absorption in three regions of the spectrum: ultraviolet, violet and yellow-green. If one percent of the aluminium ions in ruby are replaced by chromium, the yellow-green absorption gives the gem a red color.

paragraphs.heading: Fluorescence and the ruby laser
paragraphs.text: Absorbing ultraviolet, violet or yellow-green light also makes ruby give off fluorescent red light with a wavelength of 694 nanometers, which adds to its red color and perceived luster. After ruby absorbs short-wavelength light, there is a short interval when its crystal lattice is in an excited state before the fluorescence happens. If 694-nanometer photons pass through the crystal in that interval, they can trigger the emission of more fluorescent photons, in phase with them, which strengthens that red light. A ruby laser works this way: mirrors or other means send the emitted light through the crystal again and again, producing a very high intensity of coherent red light.

paragraphs.heading: Silk and stars
paragraphs.text: All natural rubies have imperfections, including color impurities and needle-shaped inclusions of rutile known as "silk". Gemologists use these needles to tell natural rubies from synthetics, simulants or substitutes. Some rubies show a three-point or six-point "star", called an asterism. It occurs when light reflects off the silk in a certain way, and such stones are cut as cabochons so the effect displays properly. This is one case where inclusions raise a gemstone's value.

paragraphs.heading: What sets the price
paragraphs.text: A ruby's quality is determined by its color, cut and clarity, and these, along with carat weight, affect its value. The shade called blood-red or pigeon blood is the brightest and most valuable red, and it fetches a large premium over other rubies of comparable quality. Almost all rubies these days are treated in some way, most commonly with heat, and the rough stone is usually heated before cutting. Untreated rubies of high quality fetch a large premium. If a ruby has no needle-like rutile inclusions at all, that may be a sign the stone has been treated.

paragraphs.heading: Ruby or pink sapphire
paragraphs.text: Generally, gem-quality corundum in every shade of red, pink included, is called ruby. In the United States, however, a stone must meet a minimum color saturation to be called a ruby; otherwise it is called a pink sapphire. Drawing this line is fairly new; it arose sometime in the 20th century. Because such distinctions are difficult and subjective, trade organizations such as the International Colored Gemstone Association have adopted the broader definition of ruby, which takes in its lighter shades, including pink.
